title: AI Selloff Drives S&P 500 Correction, Meta Muse Privacy Alarm | OWITH Daily
description:
The AI selloff pushes the S and P 500 into a correction as Nvidia drops fourteen percent, and Meta employees raise privacy alarms about the Muse AI agent. Also: big school districts push back on Google's AI Overviews, American chips serving Chinese models, Intuit sells Mailchimp, and record defense tech funding.

Good morning from OWITH.ai, the briefing that gives you only what's important to hear in AI and tech. It's Sunday, November 22.

Today, the AI selloff pushes the S and P 500 into a correction, and Meta's own staff raise privacy alarms about its Muse AI agent.

Fortune reports that the S and P 500 fell three point six percent on Friday and closed in a correction. It was the index's seventh straight loss, its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq dropped more than five percent. Nvidia fell fourteen percent, its worst day in almost two years, and is now down nearly half since early October. Goldman Sachs says any one of three things could mark a bottom: news that lifts confidence in AI earnings, a dovish signal from the Fed, or a big drop in investor positioning. That matters because futures price roughly a ninety five percent chance of a rate hike in December, so relief from the Fed looks distant and AI earnings now carry the weight of the market.

Meta employees are uneasy about Muse, the company's AI agent. Internal posts seen by Reuters and reported by Fortune describe unprompted notifications built on private data. One staffer got a reminder to reply to her sister's Signal message and wrote, "This seems like an extreme privacy violation." Another got Capital One and Charles Schwab account balances in the middle of a chat about tides for a fishing trip. A member of Meta's Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating because of prompts meant to keep users engaged. Meta says Android users must opt in to notification access. Muse has passed ten million downloads and sits at the center of Meta's AI revenue plans, while JPMorgan and Amazon are already keeping agents away from their customers.

Google faces pushback from the country's biggest school districts. Fortune reports that Google told districts their students must see AI Overviews in search results, or lose Google Search on school accounts. Chicago Public Schools says it is exploring all options, including other search providers. New York City has already disabled Gemini and AI Mode on student Chromebooks, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of using monopoly power. Los Angeles Unified has asked for a way to switch off AI summaries. Former FTC chair Lina Khan said Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. For Google, the risk is legal. Bundling AI into a dominant product invites tying claims, and Google lost a tying case over ad tech in April 2025.

On geopolitics, researchers at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology argue in a Fortune commentary that data centers full of American chips are serving Chinese AI models to users worldwide. American inference providers such as Together AI, Baseten and Fireworks run Chinese open weight models, and DeepSeek's latest model is offered by at least sixteen providers outside China, including Amazon Bedrock. Moonshot AI has reportedly asked Microsoft, Amazon and Google for thirty percent of their revenue from its Kimi K3 model. The authors argue against a ban. Their point is that exporting American infrastructure does not automatically export American models, so Washington needs its own open weight strategy.

Intuit is selling Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about three point six eight billion dollars, Fortune reports, five years after paying about twelve billion. Chief financial officer Sandeep Aujla said consumer behavior is changing faster than Intuit expected, and that more customers go to AI to get the first answer. Chief executive Sasan Goodarzi said Intuit can serve small businesses better by building AI into QuickBooks. The deal should close in early 2027, with proceeds going to share buybacks. For software executives, the message is clear. AI is forcing companies to reprice the acquisitions of the last cycle, and Intuit shares fell about thirteen percent after hours as it trimmed its revenue forecast.

Finally, defense technology. Venture investors put a record thirty seven point nine billion dollars into defense tech in the third quarter, across two hundred sixty nine deals, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune. At Fortune's Innovation Forum in Detroit, Mina Faltas of Washington Harbour Partners said the capital markets remind him of 2021. Aidan Madigan Curtis, a partner at Eclipse, described a "pretty big YOLO sentiment" in physical tech and warned of tourist investors who follow names instead of underwriting capabilities. Early stage defense startups have fetched seventeen to fifty times revenue, and the warnings arrive just as public tech stocks fall.

The thread today is trust, from investors repricing AI earnings to employees, schools and city halls deciding how far to let AI into their lives.

That's it for today. Thanks for listening to OWITH.ai. See you tomorrow.
